description: package.json, installing packages, and version numbers.

screens.body:
npm is the package manager that comes with Node. Think of it as an app store for JavaScript code.

Instead of writing everything yourself, you can install packages — bundles of reusable code other people published — with one command.

The public registry holds over a million packages: date helpers, web frameworks, testing tools, you name it.

options: Install reusable packages of JavaScript code with one command
check.question: What does npm let you do?

screens.heading: What is npm?
screens.keyPoint: npm = app store for JavaScript code. It comes with Node.

screens.body:
Every Node project starts with npm init. It asks a few questions and writes a file called package.json.

package.json is your project's ID card: its name, version, and a list of every package it depends on.

Add the -y flag (npm init -y) to skip the questions and accept the defaults. You can edit the file later.

options: A package.json file with default answers
A new user account on npmjs.com
A folder full of installed packages
check.question: What does npm init -y create?

screens.heading: npm init: your project's ID card
screens.keyPoint: npm init -y creates package.json, your project's ID card.

screens.body:
Open package.json and you'll see plain JSON. The fields that matter most:

name and version identify your project. dependencies lists the packages your code needs to run. devDependencies lists tools only developers need (like test runners).

scripts holds shortcut commands — that's the next topic's whole deal.

check.question: Where do you list a package your app needs in production?

screens.heading: Reading package.json
screens.keyPoint: dependencies = needed to run. devDependencies = needed to develop.

screens.body:
npm install <name> downloads a package into a folder called node_modules and records it in package.json.

node_modules can get enormous — thousands of files for a few packages. That's normal. Never hand-edit anything inside it.

It's also why you never commit node_modules to git. (More on that in the Project Setup topic.)

check.question: After npm install lodash, where does the code live?

code.snippet:
$ npm install lodash
added 1 package
$ ls node_modules
lodash  ...thousands of files, and that's fine

screens.heading: Installing a package
screens.keyPoint: npm install lodash → downloads it, records it, don't touch node_modules.

screens.body:
Versions look like 1.4.2 — that's MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, called semver. Each number means something.

PATCH (1.4.2 → 1.4.3): bug fixes, safe. MINOR (1.4.2 → 1.5.0): new features, still safe. MAJOR (1.4.2 → 2.0.0): breaking changes — your code might need updates.

In package.json, ^1.4.2 means "1.4.2 or any safe update" (minor + patch). ~1.4.2 means "patch updates only" — the cautious choice.

options: You stay on 1.x — major versions are breaking, so ^ won't jump to 2.0.0
check.question: Version 2.0.0 of a package comes out. You have ^1.4.2. What happens on npm install?

screens.heading: Semver: version numbers decoded
screens.keyPoint: ^ = safe updates allowed. ~ = patch fixes only.

screens.body:
Cloned a repo and there's no node_modules folder? That's correct — it's git-ignored on purpose.

Just run npm install with no arguments. npm reads package.json, downloads everything listed, and rebuilds node_modules for you.

package-lock.json pins the exact versions, so everyone on the team gets identical code. Commit the lockfile, ignore node_modules.

options: Run npm install to rebuild it from package.json
Email the previous developer for their node_modules
The project is broken — start over
check.question: You clone a project and node_modules is missing. What's the fix?

code.snippet:
$ git clone https://github.com/me/my-app.git
$ cd my-app
$ npm install   # rebuilds node_modules from package.json

screens.heading: npm install on a fresh clone
screens.keyPoint: Fresh clone? npm install (no args) rebuilds everything.

screens.body:
Some packages are tools, not ingredients: test runners, linters, bundlers. Your app doesn't need them to run — only you need them to build it.

Install those with npm install --save-dev <name> (or the shortcut -D). They land in devDependencies.

When someone deploys your app, npm can skip devDependencies to keep the install lean and fast.

check.question: You're installing a test runner nobody needs in production. Which command?

code.snippet:
$ npm install --save-dev jest
# jest is now in devDependencies — a build tool, not an ingredient

screens.heading: Dev dependencies
screens.keyPoint: --save-dev = tools for you, not ingredients for the app.
